knownFor: Presbyter of the church at Caesarea in Palestine who gathered a library of sacred books for it and, Jerome says, copied most of Origen's works with his own hand. Jailed in the Great Persecution, he worked from prison with Eusebius on a Defense of Origen, and was put to death about 310.
datesNote: No birth year is known. Arrested late in 307 (between November 307 and April 308, by A. C. McGiffert's reckoning) and held two whole years; put to death in February, which McGiffert's note on Eusebius's Martyrs of Palestine dates to 310 and the common reckoning to 309. Jerome's catalogue of writers, which lists the Defense under his name, is dated 392 or 393; Rufinus's Latin of its first book, 397
placeNote: Caesarea, a port on the coast of Roman Palestine, where he was presbyter, set up a school, gathered his library, was imprisoned and was put to death. Eusebius's longer account of the martyrdom, held only in a damaged Greek scan, has him come from Berytus, today's Beirut. A report as late as Photius has him study at Alexandria under Pierius; McGiffert thinks his teacher more probably Achillas
role: Presbyter of Caesarea; library builder and copyist of Origen's books; martyr

keyWorks.title: Defense of Origen (Apologia pro Origene)
keyWorks.about: written in prison, addressed to Christians condemned to the mines of Palestine; its first argument is that Origen searched the Scriptures as an inquirer and did not lay down doctrine. Of its six books only the first survives, in Rufinus's Latin of 397, which the Library holds in two printings. Eusebius says he and Pamphilus did the work jointly; Jerome, Rufinus, Photius and the editors differ on whose it is.

keyWorks.title: The library at Caesarea
keyWorks.about: a collection of sacred books for the church, which McGiffert says was rich in copies of Scripture, commentaries on it and Origen's works. Eusebius gave a catalogue of it in his Life of Pamphilus, now lost, so that readers could learn which of Origen's works survive. Jerome says Pamphilus bought every book Origen wrote, at great cost, and gave them to the church, and that he used the library himself.

keyWorks.title: Copies of Origen in his own hand
keyWorks.about: Jerome says he copied the greater part of Origen's works with his own hand, and wrote, about 392, that he had found twenty-five volumes of Origen's commentaries on the twelve prophets in Pamphilus's hand, which he guarded with joy. Photius says only that Pamphilus is said to have copied most of Origen's commentaries on Scripture.

traces: Eusebius sent readers to the library's catalogue for Origen's works, and A. C. McGiffert judges that Eusebius owes a large part of the materials of his history to it.
Jerome used the library: he writes that the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew was kept there, and that he found the six volumes of Eusebius's Defense of Origen there.
Jerome writes that the library was afterwards partly destroyed, and that two bishops of Caesarea, Acacius and later Euzoius, tried to restore it in parchment volumes; the second left an inventory.

Rufinus put the first book of the Defense into Latin in 397 under Pamphilus's name, and it is all that survives of the work. About 401 Jerome complained that readers gave no heed to the bishops who condemned Origen, since they thought a martyr had praised him.
Eusebius took his name and called himself Eusebius Pamphili; Jerome says the surname came from his friendship for the martyr, and McGiffert says Eusebius took it after Pamphilus's death.
remembered: Eusebius calls him his dearest friend, a man thrice dear to him, and the most illustrious of the martyrs of that time; in the longer form of his account he calls him my master, a phrase read by hand from a damaged Greek scan.

Eusebius writes that he shared his possessions with the needy; the longer form says he sold what came to him from his forebears and gave it all to the naked, the maimed and the poor, and lived without possessions.
Eusebius's Life of Pamphilus, as Jerome quotes it, says he gave the holy Scriptures freely, not only to read but to keep, to women as well as men, and kept many books ready to give away.
Socrates, a historian of the fifth century, calls Pamphilus and Eusebius trustworthy witnesses for Origen in their joint life of him and defense of him.
McGiffert writes that Pamphilus is chiefly celebrated for the library he collected at Caesarea.

uncertain: His life rests on one friend. Nearly all of it comes from Eusebius, who admired him, in the Church History and the Martyrs of Palestine. Eusebius's Life of Pamphilus in three books is lost; its one surviving passage is held only in Jerome's Latin and English, where Jerome quotes it as evidence against Pamphilus's authorship of the Defense.

Who wrote the Defense of Origen. Eusebius writes that it was written by himself and Pamphilus, who did the work jointly. Jerome, about 392 or 393, listed it under Pamphilus's name. Rufinus in 397 put its first book into Latin as Pamphilus's, though he called it the book Pamphilus is said to have written. Jerome, in Letter 84 of 400, doubted that it was Pamphilus's, saying no other work of his could be shown, and suggested it belonged to Didymus or someone else; he added, as a hostile view, that if Pamphilus wrote it, it was before he became a martyr, and that he was counted worthy of martyrdom to wash away his one fault. Rufinus answered that Jerome would no longer spare even the martyrs. About 401 to 402 Jerome said it was Eusebius's, whom he called the chief of the Arians; he had found Eusebius's six volumes in the library at Caesarea, and he charged Rufinus with changing a few statements about the Son and the Holy Spirit. He admitted he had listed it under Pamphilus's name about ten years before.

More on who wrote the Defense. Socrates calls it their joint defense and also speaks of books Pamphilus wrote. Photius, in the ninth century, says six books, five written by Pamphilus in prison with Eusebius and the sixth by Eusebius alone after Pamphilus's death. McGiffert holds it certain that Pamphilus was a joint author, and quite probable that Rufinus kept Pamphilus's explanations; he calls Jerome's treatment unfair and dishonest, as Lightfoot also pointed out. W. H. Fremantle, editor of the volume that holds Jerome and Rufinus, says Eusebius was the chief writer, sees no reason to doubt that Pamphilus was associated with him throughout, and says Pamphilus actually wrote the sixth book. Lightfoot reads the Life's statement that Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own except letters as chosen to leave out this work of compiling and partnership. Jerome's own counts differ: in the Apology against Rufinus he says Rufinus translated the first of six books by Eusebius, while in Letter 84 he says the treatise holds nearly the first thousand lines of Eusebius's sixth book; the Letter's translator notes that Jerome is again misled if the text is sound.

Whether Eusebius was in prison with him. Photius says Pamphilus wrote it shut up with Eusebius, whose Greek is held only in one sentence quoted by Delarue. Eusebius never says he was imprisoned, and McGiffert thinks it safer to suppose, with most historians, that he visited Pamphilus in prison. McGiffert calls Pamphilus Eusebius's teacher and most intimate friend, and a late Syriac chronicle in Guidi's Latin says Pamphilus taught Eusebius, who was named Pamphilus after him.

The year of his death. McGiffert's introduction says he was put to death in 309, and his note on the Martyrs of Palestine argues for February of 310 and calls the common 309 a mistake. The Library's Jerome volume notes 309 on Jerome's chapter. The translator's notice in the Ante-Nicene volume has him in prison from late 307 to the beginning of 309. Martianay's note gives 309 and February, but the day is unreadable in the scan. The census gives 307 to 310.

Where he studied. Photius says Pierius, head of the catechetical school at Alexandria, was his teacher. The translator's notice in the Ante-Nicene volume gives Berytus and study under Pierius as the common account. McGiffert says he studied at Alexandria, more probably under Achillas, and judges Photius's report on Pierius probably false, a mix of Eusebius's account and Jerome's.

His birthplace and family. That he came from Berytus, of a noble family that held public office there, stands only in Eusebius's longer account of the martyrdom, held in damaged Greek with no other print; the Syriac of the longer form is not held. McGiffert says Eusebius himself was surely its author. The shorter account, in English, does not give it.

The manner of his death. The shorter account of the martyrdom, in English, says only that the governor Firmilian punished Pamphilus and his companions like the others; the longer form in Greek says beheading, and Photius says by the sword. Twelve died in all, and Pamphilus was the only presbyter among them.

How much he copied. Jerome says the greater part of Origen's works, and Photius says he is said to have copied most of Origen's commentaries on Scripture. In Jerome's Latin, 'manu ejus' says only in his hand; Rufinus's editors Lommatzsch and Delarue read the phrase as Pamphilus's.

The end of Jerome's passage on the volumes. His Latin says the volumes seem to him to be marked with the traces of his own blood, and the English of the Library's Jerome volume follows it. The Greek of Sophronius printed beside the Latin ends with the traces of his own suffering, read from a scan with letter faults.

Copies of the Bible. McGiffert reports a colophon in a Vatican manuscript, in Lightfoot's translation, saying that Pamphilus and Eusebius corrected the copy, and Taylor's report that many copies of the fifth column of Origen's Hexapla were issued from Caesarea under Pamphilus and Eusebius. The manuscripts are not held, so both rest on editors.

Other writings. The Ante-Nicene Fathers print an Exposition of the Chapters of the Acts of the Apostles under his name, and its notice says others ascribe it to Euthalius of Sulce; it is not counted here.

Photius's view of the Defense. Photius, writing five centuries later, says it is not a refutation of the charges against Origen but rather supports the accusation, and lists fifteen charges that the Defense calls slanders. A hostile late reader, whose Greek is not held except for one sentence in Delarue.

The text of the Defense. The Greek is lost. Book I survives only in Rufinus's Latin, held in two rough scans that agree with each other, and no English of it is held. Jerome charged Rufinus with changing passages on the Son and the Holy Spirit; the passage quoted in the story is not on those subjects.

briefReferences: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, written 392 or 393, English in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers: twenty-five volumes of Origen's commentaries on the twelve prophets, in Pamphilus's hand, kept with joy; one letter of a martyr, so many thousand lines, the traces of his own blood. The story's about eighty years counts from his death about 310.

Eusebius, Church History VII.32.25 and VIII.13.6, tr. A. C. McGiffert: Pamphilus a presbyter at Caesarea. World census, Pamphilus of Caesarea: Caesarea Maritima, a port in Roman Palestine, today in Israel.
World census, Origen: the Bible scholar who taught at Caesarea in the century before and died about 253. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75: Pamphilus copied most of his works with his own hand.

Jerome, in a letter kept in Rufinus's Apology: Pamphilus bought every book Origen had written, at great cost, and gave them to the church at Caesarea. Eusebius, Church History VI.32.3: the catalogue of the library in his Life of Pamphilus.
Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 11.1-2: the giving of his possessions to the needy; the longer form in Greek: the inheritance sold and given to the poor.
Eusebius, Life of Pamphilus III, as Jerome quotes it in the Apology against Rufinus I.9: the gift of books and Scriptures to men and to women. The Life is lost.

Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 7.4-6: the governor Urbanus tests him, orders him to sacrifice, has his sides scraped in long torture, and puts him in prison. McGiffert's notes: the fifth year of the persecution, late 307, and two whole years in prison.

Eusebius, Church History VI.33.4: the Defense written by us and Pamphilus, done jointly. McGiffert's note: Eusebius spent a great deal of time with Pamphilus in prison. Photius: five books written by Pamphilus in prison with Eusebius.
The Defense, Book I, preface to the confessors, in Rufinus's Latin: Origen searching as far as his strength allows, not settling doctrine. Addressed to confessors condemned to the mines of Palestine.

Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 11.1-2 and 11.14: twelve in all, Pamphilus the only presbyter; the governor Firmilian asks if they will now obey and passes sentence. The longer form in Greek and Photius: by the sword. McGiffert's note: February of 310, against the common 309.

Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, Letter 84 and the Apology against Rufinus I, II and III; Rufinus's preface and Apology; Photius, codices 117-118: the dispute over who wrote the Defense, in the order the story tells it. McGiffert, Fremantle and Lightfoot: the modern editors.

McGiffert's introduction: Eusebius owes a large part of the materials of his history to the library; Jerome also used it. Jerome, Apology against Rufinus I.10: readers give no heed to the bishops who condemn Origen, since they think a martyr has praised him.
World census, Alexandrian Christianity: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: If it is a joy to have one letter of a martyr, how much more to have so many thousand lines! He seems to me to have marked them with the traces of his own blood.
quotationOriginals.printed: And if it is such joy to have one epistle of a martyr how much more to have so many thousand lines which seem to me to be traced in his blood.
quotationOriginals.work: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The story's English is made from Jerome's Latin, which the Library holds only in a scan with letter faults, so the printed English stands alone. The Latin says the volumes seem to him to be marked with the traces of his own blood (sui sanguinis); the Greek of Sophronius beside it, read from a scan with faults, ends with the traces of his own suffering. 'Manu ejus' says only in his hand; the editors of the Defense read it as Pamphilus's.

quotationOriginals.modern: Who among those eager to learn was not a friend of Pamphilus? If he saw any of them lacking what they needed to live, he gave freely what he could. He gave the holy Scriptures too, most readily, not only to read but to keep. He gave them not only to men, but also to women he saw devoted to reading. So he kept many books ready, to give to those who wanted them whenever need arose.
quotationOriginals.printed: What lover of books was there who did not find a friend in Pamphilus? If he knew of any of them being in want of the necessaries of life, he helped them to the full extent of his power. He would not only lend them copies of the Holy Scriptures to read, but would give them most readily, and that not only to men, but to women also if he saw that they were given to reading. He therefore kept a store of manuscripts, so that he might be able to give them to those who wished for them whenever occasion demanded.
quotationOriginals.work: Eusebius, Life of Pamphilus III, as Jerome quotes it in the Apology against Rufinus I.9, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Eusebius's Greek is lost, and the Latin that Jerome quotes is held only in a scan with letter faults, so the printed English stands alone. The story's English is made from the Latin and differs in wording: those eager to learn for lover of books, and not only to read but to keep for lend and give.

quotationOriginals.printed: We prepared this carefully and did the work jointly on account of faultfinders.
quotationOriginals.work: Eusebius, Church History VI.33.4, tr. A. C. McGiffert
quotationOriginals.original: ἣν τῶν φιλαιτίων ἕνεκα συμπονήσαντες ἀλλήλοις διὰ σπουδῆς πεποιήμεϑα
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek of these two lines is clean and read by hand; the neighboring lines of the scan have faults. McGiffert's jointly renders the Greek words for working together with one another.

quotationOriginals.modern: When he explains these things, he often adds and declares that he is not pronouncing them as a final verdict, or settling them as fixed doctrine. He is searching as far as his strength allows, and examining the sense of the Scriptures. He does not claim to have grasped it wholly and perfectly.
quotationOriginals.printed: quae cum exponit, frequenter addere solet, et profiteri se non haec quasi definitiva pronuntiare sententia, nec statuto dogmate terminare, sed inquirere pro viribus, et sensum discutere Scripturarum, nec tamen profiteri quod integre perfecteque comprehenderit
quotationOriginals.work: The Defense of Origen, Book I, in Rufinus's Latin, ed. Lommatzsch
quotationOriginals.uncertain: No English of the Defense is held, so the story's English is made from this Latin. The Migne printing of the same Latin agrees, with letter faults of its own. The Defense says this; whose words it is, Pamphilus's or Eusebius's, is disputed.
